item.content:encoded:
I realize this is potentially 3 years too late, But I just wanted to give my two cents on the subject.

It could be that the it was a typical "hidden vault"-type door, as in, the outside of the door is just a blank, featureless wall, but on the inside it is more of a proper door. If the door opened inward (as in: into the weird chamber), it would require that someone pushed the door closed from the inside.

It is also very similar to how the Pharaohs built the pyramids. The "finishing touch" was often that a couple of slaves were forced to seal the tombs from the inside, to guarantee that nobody would find a way to get in. Dead men tell no tales, after all.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really enjoyed the series but one thing is bugging me…

You must close the containment chamber. To ensure success, you must remain inside the chamber when it closes. The Foundation will honor your sacrifice and its meaning for the continued existence of the human race, but there is no chance of survival. We are sorry.

Why would it be necessary to remain inside the containment chamber to ensure success in closing the door? Who designs containment chambers like that? Sure, it makes the whole thing more poignant - the heroic self-sacrifice and all that - but it just seems like an unneccessary sacrifice.

Years ago I read an account of a sinking ship, and the sacrice made by sailors belowdecks to seal off a flooding section of the hull from within in order to try to save the ship. In this case the sacrifice really was required and it really was a poignant scene. But without that necessity (as in this story), it doesn't quite work, imho.

Still, +1 on the overall strength of it.
